strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question: whether relatively small language models can acquire transferable rule-based reasoning abilities through reinforcement learning.
The training collection covers eight datasets with varied rule formats, reasoning styles, and depths, and evaluation includes both in-distribution tasks and three held-out benchmark families.
The reported results are promising: RuleReasoner-8B improves substantially over the Qwen3 base model and consistently exceeds the matched GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO baselines.

The paper includes useful analyses of domain-weight trajectories, data quantity, model scale, rule perturbations, task difficulty, and test-time sampling, as well as prompts and major training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central DADS contribution is technically modest—essentially softmax reweighting of domains by an exponential moving average of reward—and is insufficiently distinguished from prior adaptive curricula and data-mixture optimization methods.

The algorithm contains important inconsistencies. Rewards are defined as {-1,1} in Eq. 1 but as {0,1} in Algorithm 1; domains absent from a sampled batch make the per-domain mean undefined; and adding the same epsilon inside every softmax logit cancels exactly, so it cannot provide the claimed minimum sampling weight.

Key implementation details conflict across sections: the main text reports inference temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, whereas Table 6 reports 0.8 and 1; the main text gives DADS temperature 0.5, while Table 6 gives 0.8 for the 4B model. The code and model links on the first page are empty, materially limiting reproducibility.

The efficiency evidence is not rigorous. Figure 6 uses an unclear 'proportion of each domain' axis extending to 128%, Figure 7 lacks uncertainty and compute-normalized comparisons, and the paper does not report wall-clock time, generated tokens, or total rollout cost. Thus claims of higher computational efficiency are not established.

Reported statistics and interpretations are inconsistent. Table 4 reports SFT and RuleReasoner OOD scores of 66.6 and 81.7, but the surrounding text calls 34.4 and 54.5 their OOD performance, apparently confusing gains with scores. The claimed five-run evaluation and one-sided p-values are not supported by reported p-values, and uncertainty is mostly absent for baselines and OOD results.

The generalization claim is overstated. OOD evaluation uses selected logical-deduction subsets closely related to the training tasks rather than broad unseen domains, and the authors explicitly acknowledge possible BBH leakage into Qwen3. No contamination analysis is provided.

There is no clean ablation separating historical smoothing, reward-based reweighting, temperature, target reward, and the curated task mixture. Comparisons against uniform GRPO help, but do not show which DADS components matter or whether simpler static/heuristic mixtures would perform similarly.

Several benchmark comparisons are difficult to interpret fairly because proprietary frontier models differ greatly in prompting, inference budget, and model size, while their variance is not reported. The strongest defensible evidence is therefore the matched-base RL comparison, not the headline claim of surpassing frontier reasoning models.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: improving multi-domain logical reasoning in relatively small language models using reinforcement learning.
DADS is simple, computationally lightweight, and potentially useful in practice: it prioritizes domains with low exponentially smoothed rewards without requiring a separate difficulty model.

The empirical study covers eight training domains, two model sizes, several RL and supervised baselines, and additional analyses of learning dynamics, rule noise, task difficulty, and test-time sampling.
The reported in-distribution and aggregate benchmark improvements are promising, especially for the 8B model. The paper also reports multiple seeds and some hyperparameter and infrastructure details.
The authors appropriately acknowledge limited rule coverage, uncertain scaling, and possible BBH contamination in the limitations and appendix.
weaknesses: The central OOD claim is not reliable. The training collection already includes a Logical Deduction dataset, while the BBH evaluation uses the logical_deduction subsets with three, five, and seven objects. This is severe task overlap and may also involve example overlap depending on how the cited data were processed. The authors additionally concede possible Qwen3 pretraining leakage on BBH, yet BBH remains part of the headline OOD average and produces the near-perfect 99.6% result.

The novelty is limited. DADS is essentially inverse-performance domain sampling using an exponential moving average and softmax. Closely related adaptive curriculum and mixture-selection methods are discussed, but the paper neither establishes a substantial conceptual distinction nor compares directly against strong adaptive-sampling alternatives such as ADARFT or SRPO under matched conditions.

The algorithm contains unresolved technical inconsistencies. Adding the same epsilon inside every softmax logit has no effect after normalization, contrary to the claim that it guarantees a minimum domain probability. The update is undefined when a domain has no samples in a batch, and the reward is variously specified as {-1,1} and {0,1}. These details affect the claimed behavior of the method.

The experiments do not adequately isolate DADS from data curation and multi-task RL. Essential controls are missing, including fixed uniform or dataset-proportional sampling on exactly the same curated data and compute, alternative difficulty-based samplers, and sensitivity analyses for alpha, tau, epsilon, batch size, and reward noise.

The efficiency claim is insufficiently supported. The paper mainly compares training steps and approximate curves, without reporting wall-clock time, generated tokens, total rollouts, FLOPs, confidence intervals, or numerical efficiency tables. Figure 6 shows only a small advantage over GRPO at several data proportions, and Figure 7 does not establish equal computational cost per step.

Several baseline comparisons are not fully fair or informative. A domain-specialized fine-tuned model is compared against general-purpose proprietary models; inference settings and prompt parity for those APIs are incompletely documented. Moreover, the reported DAPO baseline removes its dynamic-sampling component, weakening a particularly relevant competitor.

The paper states that five runs and one-sided significance tests are used, but the promised p-values are not reported. Most analysis figures lack uncertainty, and it is unclear whether all baselines, including proprietary systems, were independently evaluated five times.

Outcome-only exact-match rewards cannot verify or teach valid structural reasoning paths, despite claims about interpretability and learning valid reasoning steps. The trajectory evidence consists of selected examples, with no systematic evaluation of proof validity, faithfulness, shortcut use, or robustness to counterfactual rules.

Reproducibility is currently weak: the title page contains blank Code and Model links, processed data and checkpoints are not provided, and important descriptions conflict. For example, the prose gives tau=0.5 generally whereas Table 6 gives tau=0.8 for the 4B model, and batch size is described as 64 examples in one place but 65,536 tokens elsewhere.

The presentation includes overstated or erroneous interpretations. Table 4 reports raw OOD scores of 66.6 for SFT and 81.7 for RuleReasoner, but the text describes 34.4 versus 54.5, apparently confusing gains with scores. Claims of generalization to unseen tasks and rules are stronger than the three narrow, overlapping OOD evaluations justify.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: whether relatively small language models can acquire broadly transferable rule-based reasoning through reinforcement learning.
Domain-aware Dynamic Sampling is simple, computationally inexpensive, and intuitively motivated: training emphasizes domains on which the current policy receives lower historical rewards.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering eight in-distribution datasets, three out-of-distribution benchmarks, two model sizes, supervised baselines, several RLVR methods, and strong proprietary or frontier models.

The reported results are promising. In particular, RuleReasoner-8B achieves strong average ID and OOD performance, while the 4B results suggest that the approach is not limited to a single model scale.

The paper includes useful analyses of learning dynamics, training-set size, task mixtures, rule ordering and noise, problem difficulty, and test-time sampling. It also reports multiple-run results for the proposed models and provides training prompts and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The evidence does not cleanly isolate the contribution of DADS from that of the broad curated training mixture. A controlled comparison using exactly the same RL algorithm, data, compute, and uniform or fixed domain sampling should be the central ablation; the presented comparisons and task-mixture analysis do not establish this as clearly as needed.

The sampling formulation contains a technical inconsistency: adding the same epsilon inside every softmax logit, exp((v_i+epsilon)/tau), cancels during normalization and therefore cannot provide the claimed minimum sampling probability. The treatment of domains absent from a batch, for which the per-domain mean reward is undefined, is also unspecified.

Several reported quantities are internally inconsistent. The main text states five evaluation runs, whereas the hyperparameter table lists three seeds. Inference temperature and top-p values differ between the main text and appendix. Some OOD improvement claims do not agree with Table 4 or Figure 1, and the paper says it reports one-sided p-values but no p-values are visible.

Statistical comparisons are incomplete: uncertainty is shown mainly for the proposed models, not for the principal RL baselines, and significance is not established for several relatively small efficiency differences. Wall-clock time, token or rollout budgets, and uncertainty on the learning curves are insufficiently documented for strong efficiency claims.

The claim that outcome-only RL teaches valid structural reasoning paths is stronger than the evidence. Exact-match final-answer accuracy and a few qualitative trajectories do not establish reasoning faithfulness, rule adherence, or causal use of the stated rules.

Data and evaluation quality need stronger validation. One listed negative LogicNLI example marks 'entailment' as incorrect even though the queried statement appears verbatim among the facts, and another displayed training example contains entities not supported by its visible context. The appendix also acknowledges possible BBH contamination, weakening part of the OOD claim.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the title page contains empty Code and Model links, and important details such as initialization of domain reward estimates, behavior for unsampled domains, exact per-baseline training budgets, checkpoint selection, and full evaluation outputs are missing.

The method is a fairly direct reward-based curriculum over dataset domains, so its novelty relative to adaptive curriculum and data-mixture methods is incremental. Hyperparameter sensitivity and comparisons to stronger difficulty-aware or sample-level adaptive samplers would improve the positioning.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: improving multi-domain rule-based reasoning with small language models rather than relying solely on model scaling or proprietary supervision.
DADS is simple and computationally lightweight in principle, using historical domain rewards to adapt the training mixture without a separate difficulty model.

The empirical study covers eight training domains, several held-out benchmarks, two model sizes, strong RLVR and curriculum-learning baselines, hyperparameter sensitivity, task-mixing analyses, and qualitative examples.
The reported gains over GRPO, DAPO, ADARFT, and static curricula are potentially substantial, particularly on ProverQA and BigBench Extra Hard.
The authors provide prompts, dataset sources, major training hyperparameters, limitations, and an ethics discussion.
weaknesses: The central OOD claim is compromised by likely benchmark overlap. The training collection includes a Logical Deduction dataset sourced from SymbCoT, while the BBH evaluation explicitly uses BBH Logical Deduction with three, five, and seven objects. Treating the resulting 99.6% BBH score as performance on an unseen task is not justified without rigorous deduplication and provenance analysis. The paper itself also raises possible BBH leakage in Qwen3.

Several headline numbers are internally inconsistent. Table 3 reports base-model OOD performance of 34.2, whereas Tables 6 and 10 report 14.2 on the stated three OOD benchmarks. Section 4.2 confuses absolute SFT scores with improvements, and the claimed OOD gains vary across the abstract, introduction, and tables. Table 7 reports roughly 70% for the same three-benchmark OOD average under selected hyperparameters, while the main result is 81.7%, without explaining the discrepancy.

The algorithm is not specified consistently enough for reliable reproduction. Equation 1 defines rewards in {-1,1}, whereas Algorithm 1 declares {0,1}; initialization and updates for domains absent from a batch are unclear; and adding epsilon before normalization does not guarantee the claimed minimum sampling probability. Hyperparameter names and values also differ between the main text and appendix.

The evidence for computational efficiency is inadequate. Figure 7 compares training steps rather than wall-clock time, generated tokens, rollout count, or FLOPs; these are not necessarily comparable across DAPO, GRPO, and DADS. The asserted 1.4x acceleration is therefore insufficiently supported.

Uncertainty reporting is weak. The manuscript says evaluations use five runs, but it is unclear whether these are inference samples or independent training runs; the appendix lists only three seeds. Most ablations and OOD comparisons provide no error bars or significance tests, so several modest gaps cannot be assessed reliably.

The claimed generalization mechanism involving emergent meta-introspection and self-verification is inferred from a few selected trajectories rather than established experimentally. No faithfulness analysis shows that generated chains reflect the model's actual decision process.

DADS is a relatively direct inverse-reward curriculum with exponential smoothing. Given this modest methodological novelty, the paper needs especially rigorous contamination controls, consistent results, and compute-matched evaluation; the current submission does not meet that standard.

Reproducibility remains incomplete because code, processed data, exact split identities, deduplication procedures, and model checkpoints are only promised after review. Some displayed qualitative labels also appear questionable—for example, an answer directly supported by a LogicNLI fact is marked incorrect—raising additional concerns about label mappings or presentation accuracy.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: improving multi-domain rule-based reasoning with reinforcement learning while allocating training effort adaptively across domains.
The domain-aware sampling rule is simple, intuitive, and inexpensive; using exponentially smoothed rewards avoids requiring a separate difficulty model.
The evaluation is broad in nominal scope, including eight training-domain tasks, three principal held-out benchmarks, several RL/curriculum baselines, and additional reasoning tasks.
The appendices provide prompts, data sources, implementation hyperparameters, sensitivity analyses, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central out-of-distribution claim is not credible as presented. The training collection includes Logical Deduction, while the BBH evaluation explicitly uses logical-deduction subsets. The authors themselves acknowledge possible BBH leakage, yet BBH is reported as an unseen OOD task and contributes the near-perfect 99.6% result.

Reported results are internally inconsistent. The abstract claims a 10.4-point OOD advantage over o1, the introduction claims 14 points, Figure 1 implies roughly 14.3 points, and the main text elsewhere reports incompatible OOD values such as 54.5%, 81.7%, and a 47.5-point improvement. Table 7 reports approximately 70% OOD performance under selected hyperparameters, whereas Tables 6 and 10 report 81.7%, without explaining the discrepancy.

The main contribution is insufficiently isolated. The proposed model combines DADS with rule shuffling, removal of KL and entropy terms, a curated task mixture, and other training choices. A clean aggregate comparison against an otherwise identical static sampler is missing; the direct with/without-DADS analysis is restricted to AR-LSAT.

The evidence for computational efficiency is weak. Training steps and sample proportions are used as proxies, but rollout counts, discarded generations, tokens, GPU-hours, and wall-clock cost are not reported consistently. This does not substantiate claims of lower computational cost, especially across methods with different sampling procedures.

The OOD benchmarks are closely related to the training domains—e.g., ProverQA versus ProofWriter/ProntoQA and BBH logical deduction versus the Logical Deduction training set. There is no train-test deduplication, contamination audit, or sufficiently controlled compositional split.

Important experimental details conflict or remain unclear: the text states batch and minibatch sizes of 64 while the appendix gives token-based sizes; five evaluation runs are claimed while three random seeds are listed; it is unclear whether uncertainty reflects independent training runs or only stochastic inference.

The reported maximum input length is 1,024 tokens, but BBEH difficulty groups are defined using inputs as long as 2,741 tokens. The paper does not explain truncation or a different inference context limit, creating a serious reproducibility and evaluation-validity concern.
Several very large transfer gains on unrelated tasks, including AIME, GPQA, and Coin Flip, are reported without uncertainty, contamination checks, or analysis sufficient to make them convincing.

Technical presentation contains inconsistencies: the exact-match reward is defined as {-1,1} in the equation but {0,1} in Algorithm 1, handling of zero-variance GRPO reward groups is unspecified, and the assertion that exact-match rewards eliminate policy distribution shift does not justify removing KL regularization.

The novelty is limited: prioritizing domains with low moving-average reward is a straightforward hard-domain sampling heuristic. The paper provides neither a theoretical analysis nor sufficiently rigorous controlled evidence showing when it is preferable to existing adaptive sampling methods.

The claimed new 32K dataset is primarily an aggregation and transformation of existing public datasets, including reasoning traces generated by DeepSeek-R1. Its novelty, licensing, filtering quality, split construction, and exact released contents are insufficiently established, and code/data are only promised after review.

Overall, the paper has a potentially useful engineering idea, but inconsistencies, questionable OOD labeling, missing controls, and inadequate efficiency evidence undermine its main conclusions and place it below the acceptance threshold.

RULECOLLECTION-32K combines eight reasoning datasets spanning deduction, induction, first-order logic, constraint satisfaction, and analytical reasoning; this is a potentially useful training resource.

The empirical scope is substantial: the paper compares against supervised training, multiple RLVR algorithms, curriculum-learning approaches, prior rule-based reasoners, and frontier proprietary models.

The reported results are promising, particularly the improvements over GRPO, DAPO, ADARFT, balanced sampling, and easy-to-hard curricula. The 8B model also improves consistently across the reported ID domains.
The appendices provide prompts, dataset statistics, major hyperparameters, sensitivity analyses, task-mixing studies, complexity breakdowns, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The headline OOD claim is seriously compromised by the BBH evaluation. The training collection contains a “Logical Deduction” dataset with the same object-ordering task format, while the alleged OOD BBH evaluation explicitly selects BBH logical-deduction subsets with three, five, and seven objects. The paper does not establish dataset disjointness or rule out duplicated instances. It even acknowledges possible BBH leakage in the Qwen3 base model. Consequently, the near-perfect 99.6% BBH result cannot convincingly support task-level OOD generalization.

Several central numbers are internally inconsistent. Table 3 reports the base model’s OOD performance as 34.2 and RuleReasoner’s as 81.7, whereas Table 6 reports the same three-benchmark base average as 14.2 and DADS as 81.7. The surrounding text also confuses performance values with improvements, describing 34.4 versus 54.5 as OOD performance although these are the deltas in Table 3. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the quantitative conclusions.

The DADS contribution is technically modest: an EMA of per-domain rewards followed by softmax upweighting of lower-reward domains. Its relationship to established adaptive sampling, bandit allocation, and robust/group distributionally robust optimization is not developed theoretically or empirically beyond a limited collection of curricula.

Algorithm 1 is underspecified for domains absent from a sampled batch, for which the domain sample count can be zero. There are also inconsistencies between the reward range in Equation 1 ({-1,1}) and Algorithm 1 ({0,1}), and between inference/training hyperparameters stated in the main text and Appendix D.

The efficiency evidence is insufficient for the claim of computational acceleration. The claimed 1.4× improvement is inferred from optimizer-step counts rather than measured wall-clock time, generated tokens, rollout calls, or FLOPs. Figure 6’s “proportion of each domain” reaching 128% and its step-500 protocol are also inadequately explained.

OOD results and most baseline comparisons lack uncertainty estimates or statistical tests. Although the paper says evaluations use five runs, it is unclear whether these are independent training seeds or merely stochastic inference runs; baseline variance is generally omitted. This is especially consequential for small test sets such as the 67-example Clutrr and LogiQA splits.

The proposed explanation that “meta introspection,” self-simulation, and self-verification emerge during training is supported only by selected qualitative trajectories. No controlled measurement establishes this mechanism or separates it from ordinary task adaptation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete because the code, trained models, and curated dataset are only promised after review. Exact data splits, deduplication procedures, baseline hyperparameter parity, total training compute, and per-run results are not presently available.
